subject: Communication
title: Seating Arrangements and Power Dynamics
description: A 60-second lesson on Seating Arrangements and Power Dynamics.

hook.text: King Arthur used a round table to eliminate hierarchy. The shape of the table shapes the conversation.

buildup.text: Rectangular tables create power positions (head vs. sides). Round tables distribute status more evenly.

discovery.text: Research shows people seated across from each other are more likely to compete; side-by-side, they cooperate.

twist.text: Sitting at the head of a table makes you 4x more likely to be perceived as the leader — even without a title.

climax.text: Therapists sit at angles, not across — reducing confrontation. Police interrogators sit directly across.

punchline.text: Where you sit tells people who you are before you speak.

quiz.question: What seating arrangement tends to promote cooperation?
options: Facing each other across a table

details.summary: Where people sit in meetings communicates status and relationship. The head of the table signals leadership, sitting across creates opposition, and sitting at an angle promotes collaboration.
details.whyItMatters: Strategic seating can set the tone for negotiations, reduce conflict, and project or diminish authority before a word is spoken.
takeaways: Head-of-table positions signal leadership and authority
Sitting across from someone creates a competitive dynamic
Corner or side-by-side seating encourages collaboration

faq.question: How should I choose my seat in a negotiation?
faq.answer: To reduce confrontation, sit at an angle rather than directly across. To project authority, take a central position. To build rapport, sit beside the other party. The round table eliminates positional hierarchy entirely.

faq.question: Does the shape of the table matter?
faq.answer: Yes. Rectangular tables create natural head positions and hierarchy. Round tables promote equality, which is why King Arthur's legendary table was round. U-shaped arrangements direct attention to a focal point.
